name: open-adventure
why: The original Colossal Cave Adventure faithfully reproduced by Eric Raymond, a foundational text game worth an evening.

brief.what_it_is: Open Adventure is a text adventure game: a reproduction of Colossal Cave Adventure, the 1995 430-point version, which the project calls Adventure 2.5. You type short commands at a terminal prompt and read the game's text descriptions of the cave in reply. The built program is named advent, which the author chose to avoid a name clash with the BSD Games version. The project is a forward port of the Crowther and Woods code to modern systems, with the source published on GitLab under a BSD 2-Clause license.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents it as the last descendant of the original 1976 Colossal Cave Adventure that its original authors, Crowther and Woods, worked on, and says it is shipped with their permission and encouragement. The project aims to keep that foundational game playable and buildable on current systems.
brief.how_it_works: The game is a port of the original Fortran-derived code, and the recent changes note that it dropped the legacy 1-based indexing, which required a save-format version bump. The build uses make and needs libedit for line editing. The install notes say Python 3 is required because of a security issue with the YAML library, and PyYAML is used by the build.

commands_seen.context: Change into the top-level source directory before building.
Build the game from the source tree.
Optional regression test run on the code; the tests also need spellcheck.
Run the game in the terminal to play.
Install the libedit build dependency on Debian and Ubuntu.
Install the libedit build dependency on Fedora.
Alternative way to install the PyYAML library, which the Python 3 requirement involves.

brief.install_notes: Build from source: install libedit first (apt-get install libedit-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf install libedit-devel on Fedora, or the editline package from thrysoee.dk). Install PyYAML with pip3 install PyYAML, since Python 3 is now required. Then cd into the source directory, run make, optionally run make check, and start the game with ./advent. Building the documentation additionally needs asciidoctor. No accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration are mentioned. The Homebrew formula is named open-adventure and is packaged under that name.
brief.standout: It is a faithful, preserved copy of a foundational 1970s text game that the original authors endorsed, and it was carefully forward-ported rather than rewritten. The binary name advent and the note about avoiding a BSD Games collision show the care taken with the historical lineage.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists version 1.22 with a page date of 08 Jul 2026 and a Recent Changes section describing a code hardening pass and a legacy indexing removal. The INSTALL page was last updated 2026-02-01. The GitLab page shows a 0.90 version label, which I could not reconcile with 1.22 from the page text.
brief.caveats: Requires Python 3 and the libedit (editline) library at build time, so it is not a single-binary install from source. The GitLab page itself was only partly rendered, so I did not read its full README. The Recent Changes entry mentions a code hardening pass done with ChatGPT, which some readers may want to weigh. Licensing is BSD 2-Clause, per the GitLab page. I did not fetch the separate hints, history, or notes docs.

judge.reason: A carefully preserved, author-endorsed version of the original text adventure offers a hands-on encounter with a foundational game, not just historical trivia.

entry.title: open-adventure
entry.tldr: A faithful, authorized port of Colossal Cave Adventure, the 1970s cave-exploring text game that started a genre, playable as `advent` in your terminal.
entry.deeper_look:
Open Adventure is Colossal Cave Adventure, the game where you type short commands like "go north" and read what the cave says back. This is the 1995 430-point version, which the project calls Adventure 2.5. It is a forward port of the Crowther and Woods code to modern systems, not a rewrite.

The homepage describes it as "the last descendant of the original 1976 Colossal Cave Adventure worked on by the original authors - Crowther & Woods; it is shipped with their permission and encouragement." The aim is to keep a foundational game playable and buildable on current machines. The built program is called `advent`, the original PDP-10 name, and the project notes this avoids a collision with the BSD Games version.

Underneath it is a door into the history of interactive fiction. Nearly every text adventure, and a good part of how games talk to players, descends from this cave. The port is also a small lesson in software preservation: recent changes include removing the legacy 1-based indexing inherited from the Fortran-era code, which meant bumping the save-file format version.
entry.install:
brew install open-adventure
# Installs the `advent` executable. No accounts or hardware needed. If building from source instead, you need libedit, Python 3, and PyYAML.

try_this.what_happens: Starts the game at the prompt. Type short commands and read the cave's replies.

entry.whats_unique: It is the preserved lineage of the original game, endorsed by its authors, ported carefully rather than reimplemented. Even the binary name follows the historical one.
entry.caveats: Building from source needs Python 3 and libedit; the Homebrew formula handles that for you. The recent changes mention a code hardening pass done with ChatGPT, which some readers may want to weigh.
